heading: Nothing runs that a person did not run first
lede: Real crypto systems automate constantly — bots, smart contracts, scheduled jobs — and a large share of real losses trace back to code that ran unattended before anyone had actually checked the sequence by hand. HEZE's own terminal draws the line on purpose: record, run, then automate, always in that order.

grid.p: Up to eight hours away is replayed one simulated day at a time — the same proposals, the same rolls, the same result you would have gotten watching it happen, never a shortcut.
Custodians only sign on their own once told to, at the same odds a person signing by hand would face — automation changes who is at the keyboard, not the rules being followed.
A command sequence is typed and watched until it is right, replayed once to confirm it, and only then set on an interval. The macro is a transcript of a person, not a program nobody read.

note.strong: The real-world version of this mistake.
note.text: A contract that moves funds on a trigger nobody tested against every input, or a bot that was live before its first run was ever watched — both are automation that skipped the middle step. The terminal's rule exists because that step is the only one that catches a mistake before it repeats forever.

text: Automation taught as a discipline: record a sequence by hand, run it once to confirm it, only then automate it — with the away-time catch-up and auto-sign as concrete examples that already follow the rule.
